Q: A program in C# to find the n-th maximum grade point achieved by the students from the list of students A:

They're both wrong. Because the students list is not sorted, you have no idea how students[num].Grade compares to the desired output. students[num] should not appear in your logic.

Your first attempt is very close, after skipping over num-1 you need to take the next one unconditionally:

var nthHighestGrade = students
    .OrderByDescending(s => s.Grade)
    .Skip(num-1)
    .FirstOrDefault();

Q: Is it possible to not display a ~ for blank lines in Vim/Neovim? A:

You can set the fillchars value for eob to a space character and that will effectively hide it.

In Lua (Neovim 0.5+):

vim.wo.fillchars='eob: '

In VimScript:

set fillchars=eob:\

Note: Calling the above will override your fillchars value for other items as well (if set), so use this as a reference to set multiple values together:

set fillchars=eob:\ ,fold:\ ,vert:\│

Or use set fillchars+=... to append it your existing values.

Q: how can I find out which python virtual environment I am using? A:

The Short Answer

You can't!

At least not without knowing a priori, where your non-virtual installation is located. And have a way to share this info in a global environment variable, for example.

In addition the python built-in to handle venv's is catastrophically broken when it comes to tracking and finding previously created venv's. There is no command to check, so if you ever forgot the name and location of your venv, good luck and enjoy the hours of searching your entire disk! (Smart dev's have their own tools for this.)

The Long Answer

Avoiding the trivial case of just checking the standard built-in python venv variable: VIRTUAL_ENV.

Today there is a plethora of virtual environments, and they all have their own way of checking and handling their environments. In addition it obviously also depends on your OS on how these are managed. Here for Windows. Just to mention 5.

  • Pythons native venv - python -m venv
  • Nordic Semiconductor's west development environment - (pip install west)
  • Various Conda installations. - A world of horror!
  • MSYS/MINGW - also sandboxed
  • Cygwin - can be either shared system or sandboxed, but doesn't always play well when shared.

They can all live independently.

The only secure way to determine where you are at, would be to first define your "system version" (in lack of other description), in a global and exotic variable. Perhaps like this.

#-------------------
# Windows
#-------------------
# Define Temporary
$Env:READ_ONLY_SYSTEM_PYTHON="C:\path-to\python.exe"

# --OR--
# Define System Wide & Permanently
$LN='READ_ONLY_SYSTEM_PYTHON'
$LP='C:\path-to\python.exe'

[System.Environment]::SetEnvironmentVariable($LN, $LP, [System.EnvironmentVariableTarget]::Machine)

Then you can use python to test if this is the same location as given by sys.executable. However, one can imagine some hipster developers also using the native OS executable but using a pip and package environment in a venv. You'd have to check for that, in the same way, and as already mentioned by other answers.

# One liner:
# python -c "import sys; p=sys.prefix; b=sys.base_prefix; e=sys.executable;print('p: ',p,'\nb: ',b, '\ne: ',e)"

import sys
p=sys.prefix
b=sys.base_prefix
e=sys.executable

print('p: ',p,'\nb: ',b, 'e: ',e)"

# Here I am in the 'llm' venv.
# p:  C:\venvs\llm
# b:  C:\lang\Python312
# e:  C:\venvs\llm\Scripts\python.exe

# deactivate

# Here I am in native (no venv) environment:
p:  C:\lang\Python312
b:  C:\lang\Python312
e:  C:\lang\Python312\python.exe

I'll leave it as an exercise to check and compare to our environment variable with python.

The Right Answer

File a complaint to python.org, on why they don't have tooling for tracking and finding venv's. Then use 3rd party tooling, like poetry and venvlink. (Unfortunately, uv developers have also chosen to ignore the issue of keeping track of venv's, so it can't be recommended.)
